---
title: "Reclaiming Storage"
guide-section: "Core Workflows"
---

Version control for data is not free the way it is for code. A pin is a native
ref, and a native ref holds storage: an Icechunk tag keeps every chunk its
snapshot references, a Neon branch keeps its history window, an Iceberg tag
blocks snapshot expiry. Each commit adds one pin per changed object, and each
fork adds a branch. This page is the canonical home for two things: how to
**preview every store write** before it happens, and the three levers for
keeping the storage bill in check.

The rule underneath all of it: **tether's VCS history is the reference set.**
A pin, branch, or listing stays alive as long as some manifest in some commit
names it. Drop the commit and `gc` releases what it held.

## Preview before you write: plans

Every command that touches an external system -- `commit`, `new`, `gc`,
`promote`, `restore`, `drop`, `import`, `repair`, `upgrade`,
`forget-workspace` -- is a read-only *plan* followed by an *apply*:

```bash
tether commit -m "Relabel plate1" --dry-run
```

```
plan: commit (3 write(s))
                 pin  zarr/imaging  [icechunk] tether.0a1b2c3d.deb4861eb388e5f6  native ref at snapshot_id=K3F9M2A1B7C8D4E5…
              record  features      [lance] pin=record: state branch=main version=7, no native ref
              record  raw/plate1    [file] Observed: recorded, not recoverable
          vcs-commit  jj commit: 'Relabel plate1'
                      db/metrics: unchanged
```

Nothing happened: no tag, no manifest write, no VCS commit. `--json` prints the
same plan as data, and `--plan FILE` saves it. A saved plan can be applied
later, exactly as computed:

```bash
tether commit -m "Relabel plate1" --plan /tmp/commit.json   # plan only
# review, get sign-off, ...
tether commit --from-plan /tmp/commit.json                   # apply it
```

Apply re-fingerprints the planned objects first. If any moved since the plan
was made, or if the manifest set changed, the apply is refused with
`StalePlanError` and nothing is written -- re-plan and look again. The same
three flags exist on every planned command; `gc` and `drop` are dry runs by
default and need `--no-dry-run` (or `--from-plan`) to apply.

From Python the split is explicit: `repo.plan_commit(...)` /
`repo.apply_commit(plan)`, `repo.plan_new(...)` / `repo.apply_new(plan)`,
`repo.plan_gc(...)` / `repo.apply_gc(plan)`, and so on. `Plan.to_json()` and
`Plan.from_json()` round-trip. The convenience forms (`tether commit`,
`Repo.new()`, ...) plan and apply under one lock and verify at apply all the
same.

### What a plan checks before it applies

What a plan saw is recorded on the plan itself as typed `preconditions`
(`Plan.preconditions`, visible in a saved plan's JSON): the manifest hash,
this workspace's id, the head of every branch the plan will keep, reset, or
create afresh, a gc plan's VCS head and a digest of *every* visible commit (a
bookmark committed in another workspace may reference a pin it would
release), a promote's base-branch state and the state its source names. Every
`apply_*` runs them all before its first action, and the first mismatch stops
the whole apply with `StalePlanError` carrying the plan's own message -- so a
stale plan does nothing at all. A saved plan from before 0.1.0b1 (plan format
1) carries no preconditions and is refused with "re-run the plan".

What is *not* a precondition is a race during apply, handled per action: a
branch that moves after gc's preflight is kept and reported while the rest of
the plan finishes; `commit` re-fingerprints each object against one snapshot;
`promote` lands the *state* the plan reviewed, not the source branch's head at
apply time, so a fork write that slips in between is not promoted by accident;
a lazy fork on first writable `open` resets an existing branch only onto the
head `new` reviewed and agreed to reset.

The one store write without a dry run of its own is that lazy fork: `open`
creates the branch `new` decided on. `new --eager --dry-run` previews what
would be created.

## Lever 1: do not pin what you will not need -- `--pin record`

Forking needs a *source*, not a *pin*. When you branch off to try something and
only care about the two heads afterwards -- not about recovering the exact
split point next year -- the tag at the split point is pure cost. Register the
object with `--pin record`:

```bash
tether add features s3://bucket/features.lance --kind lance --pin record
tether add zarr/imaging s3://bucket/imaging --kind icechunk --pin record
```

With `pin = "record"` on any backend:

- `commit` records the state (snapshot id, version, commit hash, LSN) but
  creates **no native ref**. The plan shows `record ... pin=record` instead of
  `pin`.
- `new` forks **straight from the recorded state**: `create_branch(name,
  snapshot_id)` in Icechunk, `(branch, version)` in Lance, the commit id in
  lakeFS/Dolt/git, the LSN on the branch it was read from in Neon.
- `verify` checks the state is still reachable natively; `open -r` still works
  while it is.

The trade: recoverability is now bounded by the system's own retention.
Icechunk's snapshot lives until someone expires it, Iceberg's until snapshot
expiry runs, Neon's until the history window closes. `verify --all-history`
turns each expiry into a `MISSING` report, so you always know which old
commits have become labels without data. Mix per object: keep `--pin native`
on the archive-quality store, use `record` on the scratch ones.

## Lever 2: drop history you no longer want

Suppose an experiment produced five commits, and only the last matters. Every
one of the four intermediate commits holds pins.

The one-step way is `tether abandon`: it drops the commits in the VCS and
shows the `gc` plan for what that freed, in the same breath.

```bash
tether abandon krlwtmzy ptnwqsyu        # jj change ids, or git shas
```

```
abandoned 3c1e9f0a2b7d, 8d2f4a1b9c0e
plan: gc (2 write(s))
               unpin  zarr/imaging  [icechunk] tether.0a1b2c3d.7d1e0c9a2b34e5f6  no manifest in history references it
               unpin  db/metrics    [neon] tether.0a1b2c3d.7d1e0c9a2b34e5f6  no manifest in history references it
(not applied; `tether gc --no-dry-run` releases these, or re-run with --gc)
```

Later commits keep their manifests exactly as they were -- a manifest records
a whole state, so removing an earlier one must not conflict with it (a plain
`jj abandon` or `git rebase` would). Under git the commits must be on the
current branch and the tree clean. The abandon itself is the VCS's to undo
(`jj undo`, the reflog); tether's `undo` refuses it, and if you bring the
commits back before running `gc` nothing was lost.

The VCS's own tools work too, followed by `tether gc`:

::: {.panel-tabset}

### jj

```bash
jj log -r 'main..@'
# ○  vqmxzkwl  Scores for A1, third try
# ○  ptnwqsyu  Scores for A1, second try
# ○  krlwtmzy  Scores for A1, first try
# ○  ntsyulyo  Relabel plate1 with model v3
# ◆  main

# Keep the split point and the result; fold the tries into the result.
jj squash --from krlwtmzy::ptnwqsyu --into vqmxzkwl
```

`jj squash` (and `jj abandon`) hide the old commits: they are no longer in
`all()`, which is what `gc` walks. `jj op log` can still restore them for a
while -- but once `gc` runs, a restored commit will point at pins that are
gone, and `verify` will say so.

To drop a whole side branch, `tether drop try-model-v2` does the VCS half
(`jj abandon` of the commits only it reaches, then the bookmark) and the
store half in one step -- see [`drop`](07-cli.qmd#drop). By hand it is:

```bash
jj bookmark delete try-model-v2
jj abandon 'try-model-v2-change-id::'    # everything from there up
```

### git

```bash
git log --oneline main..HEAD
# 9e1c3a0 Scores for A1, third try
# 5b77d21 Scores for A1, second try
# c0ffee1 Scores for A1, first try
# a1b2c3d Relabel plate1 with model v3

git rebase -i a1b2c3d      # mark the two middle commits `fixup`/`drop`
```

To drop a whole side branch: `tether drop try-model-v2`, or by hand `git
branch -D try-model-v2`. `gc` walks `rev-list --all`, so anything unreachable
from a ref is gone as far as tether is concerned; git's own reflog and `git
gc` are independent of that.

:::

History is now three commits. The pins that only the dropped commits named are
orphans.

## Lever 3: `gc`

```bash
tether verify --all-history      # confirm what is still referenced actually resolves
tether gc                        # dry run: the plan
```

```
plan: gc (5 write(s))
               unpin  zarr/imaging  [icechunk] tether.0a1b2c3d.7d1e0c9a2b34e5f6  no manifest in history references it
               unpin  zarr/imaging  [icechunk] tether.0a1b2c3d.c48b2f6e1d07a9b0  no manifest in history references it
               unpin  db/metrics    [neon] tether.0a1b2c3d.7d1e0c9a2b34e5f6  no manifest in history references it
               unpin  db/metrics    [neon] tether.0a1b2c3d.c48b2f6e1d07a9b0  no manifest in history references it
      delete-listing                a1c9…e3f2.jsonl  unreferenced
```

Two tags in Icechunk, two branches in Neon, one content listing. Nothing named
by the three surviving commits appears -- and nothing that belongs to another
dataset: every ref carries the dataset's id (`0a1b2c3d` here) and `gc` only
looks inside its own namespace. Had another dataset pinned the same Icechunk
repo, the plan would say `zarr/imaging: 2 pin(s) of other datasets left alone`
and stop there. Apply it:

```bash
tether gc --no-dry-run
```

```
unpinned 4 pin(s)
  icechunk: 0a1b2c3d.7d1e0c9a2b34e5f6
  icechunk: 0a1b2c3d.c48b2f6e1d07a9b0
  neon: 0a1b2c3d.7d1e0c9a2b34e5f6
  neon: 0a1b2c3d.c48b2f6e1d07a9b0
deleted 1 orphan listing(s)
```

Or save the plan and apply it from a job with the right credentials:

```bash
tether gc --plan /tmp/gc.json
tether gc --from-plan /tmp/gc.json
```

`gc` is the one command whose store writes cannot be undone: `tether undo`
after a `gc` restores the working refs it forgot and the listings it deleted
(from the VCS), and reports the released pins and deleted branches as
irreversible. If you restore a commit that references a released pin --
`jj undo` of the abandon -- `tether repair` recreates the pin from the
manifest's state, as long as the
system has not expired that snapshot yet. That window is the argument for
running `gc` some time *after* the history edit, not in the same breath.

Releasing a tag or branch makes the data *eligible* for reclamation; the
system decides when. Icechunk needs `repo.expire_snapshots(...)` then
`repo.garbage_collect(...)`; Iceberg needs `expire_snapshots`; Lance needs
`cleanup_old_versions`; Neon frees the branch's history on its own schedule.
Those are the system's operations, not tether's.

### Branches of bookmarks that are gone

Every bookmark gets a `tether.ws.<dataset>.<bookmark>` branch in each Forkable
system it writes to. A bookmark deleted with `jj bookmark delete`, renamed, or
left behind on a wiped machine leaves those branches behind, each holding
whatever it wrote. A plain `gc` never deletes a branch, so a branch you forgot
about is never why data disappears.

`gc --prune-bookmarks` is the sweep. It finds the `tether.ws.*` branches in
each system, keeps those of every bookmark the VCS still has or a live
checkout still works on (plus any `--keep-bookmark NAME`, for a bookmark that
only exists on another machine), and judges the rest by their head. Branches
from before bookmarks existed -- one per workspace and object -- are judged
the same way:

| Head state | Decision |
| --- | --- |
| natively pinned by some commit (a tag holds it) | `delete-branch` |
| equal to the base branch's head (nothing was ever written) | `delete-branch` |
| has writes no commit pinned | `keep-branch` |
| a `--pin record` state (only this branch keeps it reachable) | `keep-branch` |
| on a backend whose branches *are* the storage (Neon) | `keep-branch` |

```bash
jj bookmark delete relabel                        # the line of work is over
tether gc --prune-bookmarks                       # its branches, everywhere
tether gc --prune-bookmarks --keep-bookmark hpc   # a bookmark that lives only on the cluster
```

```
plan: gc (1 write(s))
       delete-branch  zarr/imaging  [icechunk] tether.ws.0a1b2c3d.relabel  bookmark relabel (gone); head is pinned
         keep-branch  features      [lance] tether.ws.0a1b2c3d.relabel  bookmark relabel (gone); kept: has unpinned writes (branch=tether.ws.… version=9) (--force-prune deletes)
         keep-branch  db/metrics    [neon] tether.ws.0a1b2c3d.relabel  bookmark relabel (gone); kept: branch is storage; deleting reclaims its data (--force-prune deletes)
                      keeping live bookmarks: hpc, main
```

Add `--no-dry-run` to apply. The kept branches are the decision that is yours
to make: pin what is on them (`tether new -b NAME` on a commit, then `commit`),
or decide the data is disposable and pass `--force-prune`, which deletes every
stray branch regardless -- the plan marks those `FORCED although it has
unpinned writes` so the loss is explicit before it happens:

```bash
tether gc --prune-bookmarks --force-prune --no-dry-run
```

`tether forget-workspace [ID]` retires a *checkout*: its `workspace.toml` and
`ops.jsonl` go and the VCS forgets it. Branches belong to bookmarks, not
checkouts, so it touches none; the bookmark it was on stays live for `gc` as
long as the VCS has it. `tether remove` never deletes anything either: it
leaves the object's working ref in `.tether/workspace.toml`, a plain `gc`
forgets the ref, and the branch itself is evaluated by the next
`--prune-bookmarks` like any other stray. (Lance refuses to delete a branch a
tag still points at; tether leaves it and moves on.)

### Stores tether created

::: {.callout-warning title="Experimental"}
Everything in this section -- `add --create`, `Repo.create`,
`gc --delete-stores`, `--store` -- lives in `tether.experimental.lifecycle`.
It is the one operation in tether with no `repair` path (a deleted pin can be
recreated from a manifest; a deleted store cannot), and it has not yet run
against the resources it was written for: an S3 prefix, a second clone with a
real remote. The rules below err toward keeping; the commands say so when you
use them. What has to be true before it graduates is listed in the module's
docstring.
:::

Everything above releases *refs* inside stores that existed before tether
saw them, and tether never deletes such a store. A store made with
`tether add KEY LOCATOR --kind KIND --create` (or `repo.add(..., create=True)`;
`repo.create(key, kind, locator)` makes, registers, and opens in one call) is
different: tether made it, so tether may take it away again once it is plainly
garbage. The use case is an ephemeral environment: one actor forks what it
needs, creates the stores it needs, tests, and throws the whole thing away,
leaving the world as it found it. Two things record what tether made,
neither of them in history:

- **An owner marker in the store**, written at creation and naming the dataset
  (Icechunk repository metadata, `git config tether.owner`, a `.tether-owner`
  file in a directory). Manifests are untrusted input -- a clone can say
  anything -- so a manifest never authorizes a delete; only the marker does.
- **A repository-wide index**, `tether-created.jsonl` next to the repository
  lock in the VCS's shared store (`.jj/repo/` or `.git/`): shared by every
  checkout of this clone, never committed. History cannot hold this memory:
  when a fork is abandoned, its commits -- and the manifest that named the
  store -- vanish, and nothing would remember the store exists.

`gc --delete-stores` considers these stores last, after the pin and branch
decisions. It is opt-in: a deleted store has no `repair`, and `gc` only knows
the history this clone has fetched. A store is planned for `delete-store`
only when all five hold:

1. its owner marker names this dataset (a marker naming another dataset is
   noted and left alone; a store with no marker is only dropped from the
   index -- `forget-store`);
2. no manifest in visible history, in this working tree, or in any live
   checkout's working tree names it;
3. every ref of *this dataset* in it is one this clone can account for: a
   `tether.ws.*` branch of the bookmark the store was created on (the index
   remembers it), of a live bookmark, or of one that a `new` in any live
   checkout of this clone made; and a pin that some `commit` or `repair` in a
   live checkout recorded. Anything else -- a branch of a bookmark this clone
   never had, a pin no commit of this clone made -- may be another clone or
   environment that fetched the probe and is working in the store, on the
   same bookmark or its own; its commits are not in your history, so nothing
   else would protect it. The plan then touches *nothing* in that store, your
   own pins included, and says so;
4. everything of tether's in it is released by the same plan -- its pins are
   unpinned, and its accounted-for branches are deleted under the
   `--prune-bookmarks` rules above (without `--prune-bookmarks` a branch
   blocks the store; with unpinned writes it needs `--force-prune`);
5. the backend confirms that nothing else remains: the base branch at its
   initial state, the marker, the refs the plan is about to delete, and --
   for a store with a working area, such as a git checkout -- no uncommitted
   files. `None` (cannot tell) means keep.

Otherwise the plan carries a `keep-store` that names what is in the way --
a branch or pin of another dataset, a branch of a bookmark you never had,
writes on the base branch, a backend that cannot tell. `delete-store` runs
after every other action, behind a `store_empty` precondition that is asked
again with nothing ignored right before the delete, and the backend checks
owner and emptiness once more inside `delete_store` itself; a tag or branch
that appeared in between stales the plan and nothing in it runs. `undo gc`
reports a deleted store as irreversible.

```bash
tether gc --prune-bookmarks --delete-stores               # shows delete-store / keep-store
tether gc --prune-bookmarks --delete-stores --no-dry-run  # ...and applies it
tether gc --prune-bookmarks --delete-stores --force-prune # ...overriding rules 3 and 4
```

Fetch every bookmark before you run it: a bookmark another clone pushed is a
reference `gc` can only count once it is in your history.

Two more indexes and one escape hatch round this out:

- **Stores this clone touched.** Every store a checkout of this clone forks a
  branch in or pins is recorded in `tether-touched.jsonl` beside the created
  index (always, so the record is complete by the time the feature
  graduates). `gc --delete-stores` releases this dataset's dead refs in those
  stores even when no manifest names them any more -- which is exactly the
  state an abandoned bookmark leaves behind. So when another actor writes
  ephemeral refs into *your* created store and then abandons them, *their*
  next `gc --delete-stores` cleans their refs out (their `gc` respects rule 3
  the same way: a branch or pin their clone cannot account for stops them),
  and your next one finds the store empty and finishes. An entry is dropped
  (`forget-touched`) once nothing of the dataset's is left in the store.
- **A store whose creator is gone.** An ephemeral environment's clone can die
  with its created index. Any clone of the dataset can still reclaim such a
  store by naming it -- `gc --delete-stores --store KIND=LOCATOR` (repeatable;
  `LOCATOR` is the positional locator, the `uri`) -- under exactly the same
  five rules, the owner marker in the store being the authority. A store with
  no marker is refused whoever asks.

```bash
tether gc --prune-bookmarks --store icechunk=s3://bucket/probes/emb.icechunk --no-dry-run
```

Two consequences worth knowing. A clone of the dataset on another machine has
its own (empty) index and does not reclaim the stores *you* created on its
own -- it can be told to, by locator. And a store created on the trunk and
written to through its base branch is kept forever by rule 5 (writes on the
base branch are not tether's refs); create on a bookmark when you mean to
throw the store away.

## Recap

- Plans: `--dry-run` shows store writes; `--plan FILE` saves them;
  `--from-plan FILE` applies them and refuses if anything moved.
- `--pin record` skips the native ref on any backend and forks from the
  recorded state; cheaper, retention-bound.
- Drop commits with `tether abandon`, `tether drop`, or the VCS's own
  `squash` / `abandon` / `rebase -i`; tether reads the VCS's idea of history,
  so what you cannot see it does not protect.
- `gc` releases orphaned pins and listings and never deletes a branch on its
  own; `--prune-bookmarks` deletes gone bookmarks' branches only when a tag
  already holds their head (or nothing was written); `--force-prune` deletes
  them regardless. Reclaiming the bytes is the system's own expiry step.
- A store `add --create` made is deleted by `gc --delete-stores` once nothing
  references it and only tether's own refs remain; the owner marker in the
  store and the untracked index in your repository decide, never a manifest.
